{"status":"ok","message-type":"work-list","message-version":"1.0.0","message":{"facets":{},"total-results":132018,"items":[{"DOI":"10.2139/ssrn.4918035","title":["Large Language Model-Based Planning Agent with Generative Memory Strengthens Performance in Textualized World"],"abstract":"Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being integrated into instruction-driven task planning within various external environments, such as games, compilers, and Application Programming Interfaces. Obtaining planning scenarios from Large Language Model(LLM) greatly mitigates the time and computational costs associated with rule-based and network-based approaches, but still suffers from limited contextual horizons and a lack of real-time cognitive and interactive capabilities with real environments. The engineering application point of this paper is: To address the challenges, we introduce a large language model-based task planning agent to facilitate human-computer interaction and application of LLMs in real-world task planning activities, which has a generative memory (GM-Agent) that responds to the textualized reality of planning events. The contribution in GM-Agent leverages the inherent rules and worldviews extracted from textual data, employing generative memory modules to assimilate planning knowledge from expert experiences. This framework has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in four out of five tasks set by LandWar, matching the performance of the Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback(RLHF) model in knowledge quiz tasks, despite having an equivalent number of parameters. Additionally, we have performed comprehensive comparison and ablation studies involving LLMs and various configurations, providing a detailed analysis of performance influencers and highlighting areas requiring further exploration.","author":[{"ORCID":"https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0711-6930","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"JY","family":"L","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"ORCID":"https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1526-7889","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Wenning","family":"Hao","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"kai","family":"Cheng","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Dawei","family":"Jin","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"published":{"date-parts":[[2024]]}},{"DOI":"10.1007/s10994-019-05864-5","title":["Improving coordination in small-scale multi-agent deep reinforcement learning through memory-driven communication"],"abstract":"Abstract Deep reinforcement learning algorithms have recently been used to train multiple interacting agents in a centralised manner whilst keeping their execution decentralised. When the agents can only acquire partial observations and are faced with tasks requiring coordination and synchronisation skills, inter-agent communication plays an essential role. In this work, we propose a framework for multi-agent training using deep deterministic policy gradients that enables concurrent, end-to-end learning of an explicit communication protocol through a memory device. During training, the agents learn to perform read and write operations enabling them to infer a shared representation of the world. We empirically demonstrate that concurrent learning of the communication device and individual policies can improve inter-agent coordination and performance in small-scale systems. Our experimental results show that the proposed method achieves superior performance in scenarios with up to six agents. We illustrate how different communication patterns can emerge on six different tasks of increasing complexity. Furthermore, we study the effects of corrupting the communication channel, provide a visualisation of the time-varying memory content as the underlying task is being solved and validate the building blocks of the proposed memory device through ablation studies.","author":[{"ORCID":"https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0314-8057","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Emanuele","family":"Pesce","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Giovanni","family":"Montana","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"published":{"date-parts":[[2020,1,23]]}},{"DOI":"10.20944/preprints202512.2748.v1","title":["Contextual Trust Evaluation for Robust Coordination in Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems"],"abstract":"Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for tackling complex tasks that exceed individual agent capabilities. However, existing approaches often suffer from coordination inefficiencies, a lack of trust mechanisms, and suboptimal role assignment strategies. This paper presents a novel trust-aware coordination framework that enhances multi-agent collaboration through dynamic role assignment and context sharing. Our framework introduces a multi-dimensional trust evaluation mechanism that continuously assesses agent reliability based on performance history, interaction quality, and behavioral consistency. The coordinator leverages these trust scores to dynamically assign roles and orchestrate agent interactions while maintaining a shared context repository for transparent information exchange. We evaluate our framework across eight diverse task scenarios with varying complexity levels, demonstrating significant improvements over baseline approaches. Experimental results show that our trust-aware framework achieves a 87.4% task success rate, reducing execution time by 36.3% compared to non-trust-based methods, while maintaining 43.2% lower communication overhead. The framework's ability to adapt agent roles based on evolving trust scores enables more efficient resource utilization and robust fault tolerance in dynamic multi-agent environments.","author":[{"given":"Kangning","family":"Gao","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Haotian","family":"Zhu","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Rui","family":"Liu","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Jinming","family":"Li","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Xu","family":"Yan","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Yi","family":"Hu","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"published":{"date-parts":[[2025,12,31]]}},{"DOI":"10.21203/rs.3.rs-10732437/v1","title":["A Simple and Reproducible Rat Model of Urethral Spongiofibrosis: Evaluation of Colchicine as a Potential Antifibrotic Agent"],"abstract":"Abstract

Objective Urethral stricture is an abnormal narrowing of the anterior urethra caused by fibrosis of the surrounding corpus spongiosum. Since fibrosis is the main factor responsible for disease progression, this study investigated the effect of colchicine, a drug with known antifibrotic properties, on fibrosis development in a rat model of urethral injury. Materials and Methods Twenty male Wistar-Albino rats (250–300 g) were included. One rat was used to standardize the trauma model. The remaining 19 rats were divided into control (n = 2), sham (n = 5), and treatment (n = 12) groups. No intervention was performed in the control group. Urethral trauma was induced at the 12 o’clock position in the sham and treatment groups. The treatment group additionally received oral colchicine (1 mg/kg/day). All animals were sacrificed on day 28. Histopathological evaluation of proximal (location A) and distal (location B) urethral segments included fibrosis, mononuclear cell infiltration, and vascular proliferation. Results Significant differences among groups were observed at location A for fibrosis (p = 0.013) and vascular proliferation (p = 0.020). No significant differences were detected at location B or in the combined analysis. Comparison of the sham and treatment groups showed significant differences at location A for fibrosis (p = 0.037) and vascular proliferation (p = 0.048), mainly reflecting lower scores in the sham group. No significant differences were found at location B. Conclusion The proposed rat model successfully induced urethral fibrosis, particularly in the proximal urethra. Colchicine did not demonstrate a protective antifibrotic effect under the study conditions. Larger experimental studies are required to clarify its potential role in urethral stricture treatmentKeywords: urethral stricture, fibrosis, colchicine, urethra, antifibrotic therapy

","author":[{"given":"RAMAZAN SAMET","family":"CETINKAYA","sequence":"first","affiliation":[{"name":"Kastamonu University"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"MUMTAZ","family":"DADALI","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"Ahi Evran University"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"published":{"date-parts":[[2026,8,31]]}},{"DOI":"10.64898/2026.09.11.751004","title":["From Prompt to Pipeline: A Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Model Coding Agents for Reproducible Bioinformatics Pipeline Construction"],"abstract":"Abstract Agentic coding systems are increasingly presented as a way to reduce the engineering burden of scientific software development. Bioinformatics is a strong test case for this claim because useful pipelines must combine domain-specific analysis choices, command-line software, sample metadata, workflow orchestration, container or HPC execution, and interpretable quality-control reporting. We evaluated three agentic systems - Biomni, Claude Code, and Codex - on the same task: constructing a Nextflow DSL2 pipeline for paired-end CUT&Tag data that included read QC, trimming, alignment, filtering, duplicate removal, signal track generation, per-sample and group-level peak calling, control-aware group merging, annotation, FRiP calculation, deepTools visualizations, and final MultiQC reporting. Each system received the same detailed CRAFT-style prompt and was assessed against a hand-coded reference pipeline developed by the authors. All three systems produced pipeline implementations that appeared plausible at the level of documentation and file structure, but none fully satisfied the requested analysis. The most consequential failure was shared: the agent-generated pipelines performed some form of group-level merging but did not produce the requested merged-group reporting outputs. Sample-level MultiQC reports also disagreed with the reference report. Codex was closest to the reference for primary mapped-read counts, although its total-read accounting and report structure still differed. Claude Code produced the broadest final report, but its mapping summary mixed stages and therefore could not be treated as numerically correct. Biomni produced the strongest subjective documentation, but its read-count agreement with the reference report was poor and several failures required substantial Nextflow expertise to diagnose. These results suggest that current coding agents can accelerate scaffolding, documentation, and routine implementation, but they do not eliminate the need for expert review in bioinformatics workflow construction. For complex sequencing workflows, prompts must specify not only the biological intent, but also the exact stage semantics, acceptance tests, metadata contracts, expected report sections, resource propagation rules, and failure criteria needed to distinguish a plausible pipeline from a correct one. Author summary Modern AI coding agents can write large amounts of software from natural language instructions. This study asks whether that ability is enough to build a real bioinformatics pipeline for CUT&Tag sequencing data. The answer from this evaluation is mixed. The agents produced impressive-looking pipelines and documentation, but the outputs did not fully match a hand-coded reference workflow. Most importantly, the pipelines did not generate the requested merged-group reports, which were central to the biological use case. Some errors were simple programming issues, but others required a working knowledge of Nextflow, sequencing QC, and chromatin profiling workflows. The practical conclusion is not that these tools are useless. Rather, they are best viewed as accelerators for experienced users. A biology student with little programming or workflow-management background would still have difficulty detecting and fixing the most important errors.
